summary_does_it_work: With Gemini on 50 held-out test cases, scored against the team’s hand labels: 90% decision accuracy (single-prompt baseline 88%, a tie on judgement), 100% eligibility (baseline 68%), no invented clause IDs, 2 of its 5 wrong answers sent to a person, 90% of citations support the decision (AI-checked). About 9 seconds and 1.8 LLM calls per case.
summary_which_model: Gemini Flash-Lite is the judge. Two local 8B models (Llama 3.1, Qwen 3) on our 8 GB GPU got only 54% and 52%: they refund almost every case that should be declined. The agent is ahead of a single prompt with every model, though no gap is statistically significant on 50 cases. In the cloud app, OpenAI GPT-5.4 mini (an unpaid key) only takes over when a Gemini call fails; it is not part of the comparison.
timeline_outcome: Gemini: agent 90%, baseline 88% (hand labels). Llama 3.1 8B: 54% vs 34%. Qwen 3 8B: 52% vs 44%. Gemini stays the judge
design_tool_bullet: The judge can call a tool. If the retrieved clauses do not cover a gap, the judge returns search queries for search_policy as structured JSON, code runs them and the graph loops back to it (a structured-output tool call, so it works the same with every provider). With per-gap retrieval up front, no model needed it on the test set; when we removed per-gap retrieval, a planning step called the tool on its own (section 8.6). The tool is a safety net, not the main source of clauses.
model_row_gemini: Best judgement by far (90% agent accuracy); 9 s a case including free-tier pacing. The daily quota covers about one full test run
model_row_llama: Open model on our own PC, no data leaves it. 54% agent accuracy; refunds almost everything. Default local model: level with Qwen, faster, and fits fully on the 8 GB GPU
model_row_qwen: Open model on our own PC. 52% agent accuracy; refunded 20 of 21 cases that should be declined. 6.9 GB in memory, so 11% ran on the CPU
hardware: Local models ran on one desktop: Intel Core i5-13400F, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti with 8 GB of GPU memory, Windows 11, Ollama with 4-bit models. 8 GB of GPU memory limits us to models of about 8 billion parameters. We used a 10,240-token context window: it fits the largest prompt (6,800 tokens) and keeps Llama fully on the GPU (a 16k window pushed 13% onto the CPU). Larger open models would run mostly on the CPU, several times slower, and all comparison runs had to finish in one night.
how_to_read: How to read this. With Gemini the two are tied on judgement: 5 cases only the agent got right and 4 only the baseline got right (exact McNemar p = 1.00). They are equal on borderline cases (80%) and the single prompt is slightly ahead on clear ones (97% against 93%). The agent’s clear gain is on the rules: the baseline called 2 of the 5 ineligible cases eligible and marked 14 eligible cases ineligible. Escalation is not a like-for-like comparison: the agent’s review step sends 2 of its 5 mistakes to a person, while the baseline counts as escalated only when its confidence is below 0.7 (1 of 6); and the agent’s 94% on cases not escalated includes the 5 ineligible cases the rules decide. The baseline leans towards refunding (81% of seller wins right); the agent leans towards declining (83% of buyer wins, 96% of seller wins). Against the brief’s targets: accuracy ≥ 80% met, eligibility 100% met (guaranteed on our data, because the cases’ order facts come from the same rules), citation ≥ 90% not yet shown (the AI check gives 90%, but no person has checked it), gain over baseline positive but small.
tool_use_row: Never called in the default design: per-gap retrieval already supplied the clauses (0 of 45 judged cases with Gemini, Llama and Qwen alike). Offered as an optional field in the agent-driven design it was also never used (0 of 40 Llama and 0 of 10 Gemini cases; reports/tool_field_experiment.md), so that design got its own planning step; then it is used (section 8.6)
comparison_intro: The professor asked us to try different models and explain our conclusion. We kept everything else fixed (the 50 test cases, prompts, decision guide, code, temperature 0) and changed only the model that does claim matching and judgement: Google’s gemini-flash-lite-latest in the cloud; two widely used open 8-billion-parameter models, Meta’s Llama 3.1 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3 (thinking off), running on our own PC through Ollama. OpenAI’s gpt-5.4-mini is not compared: it is only the cloud app’s fallback, and our unpaid key (OpenAI’s free usage tier, about 50 requests a day) is far short of the roughly 500 requests a test run needs. Each ran the full agent and the single-prompt baseline. Full tables: reports/model_comparison.md.
comparison_found: Gemini is far better at the judgement; the local models get about half right. Their failure is one-sided: of the 21 eligible cases that should be declined, Gemini’s agent refunded 1, Llama’s 19 and Qwen’s 20, including change-of-mind and damage-after-delivery claims. They do not apply the policy’s exclusions, and their claim matching labels ordinary complaints as defects.
comparison_bullets: The agent is ahead of the single prompt with every model (+2 points with Gemini, +20 with Llama, +8 with Qwen), but no gap is statistically significant on 50 cases: with Gemini it is a tie (5 cases only the agent got right against 4, exact McNemar p = 1.00), and the largest, Llama’s, is 17 against 7 (p = 0.06). The eligibility rules in code are 100% right with every model, while the single prompt gets 68%, 86% and 90%; on clear cases Llama goes from 37% to 60%.

Citations: the agent’s final answers never cite a clause the judge was not shown, with any model. Before that check Qwen cited BPR-05, a real clause it had not been given, in 10 of 45 judged cases; the check removed it and escalated those cases. Llama’s single prompt pasted the clause heading into every citation (a real clause in the wrong format, counted separately).

Escalation: Gemini’s agent escalates 6% of cases (asking for more evidence, or low confidence) and 2 of its 5 mistakes are among them; it is right on 94% of the cases it does not escalate (including the 5 ineligible cases the rules decide). Qwen’s 22% is almost entirely the BPR-05 citations (10 of 11), not low confidence; the local models never reported low confidence on their mistakes, so with them escalation only catches bad citations.

Speed: 9 s a case with Gemini (including the free tier’s pacing of at least 4.5 s between calls), 15 s with Llama, 19 s with Qwen (agent, median). Local models cost nothing per call and keep case data on the machine.
comparison_choice: Gemini Flash-Lite is the judge: it is by far the most accurate of the models we tested (90% against 54% and 52%, and 94% on cases it does not escalate), and it is free. The local 8B models are not good enough to judge on their own: they would refund nearly every dispute, which hurts honest sellers. Llama 3.1 8B is the default local model (level with Qwen, faster and fully on our GPU), an option when data must stay on the machine, not a replacement. OpenAI GPT-5.4 mini only keeps the cloud app running when a Gemini call fails (an unpaid key, about 50 requests a day); its judgements were not tested, so the app marks them as fallback answers.
comparison_hardware: 8 GB of GPU memory limited us to 8B models at 4-bit. Llama took 6.1 GB and ran fully on the GPU; Qwen took 6.9 GB and ran 11% on the CPU. 14B-and-larger models, which might close the gap, would have run mostly on the CPU, several times slower, and every run had to finish in one night. The local default was picked on the test set, so its numbers are slightly optimistic. So “cloud vs local” is also “a strong small cloud model vs 8B models at 4-bit”; the comparison cannot separate the two.
retrieval_intro: Does retrieval change the decisions, or only the citations? We ran three designs of the agent on the local models (free to run): per gap (the default), agent-driven (only general clauses up front; a planning step decides which gaps they miss and calls search_policy, then the judge decides) and none (no clauses at all). Gemini was probed on 10 cases to save the free quota.
retrieval_found: With our full decision guide, retrieval barely changes the local models’ accuracy: per gap 54% / 52%, agent-driven {la} / {qa}, none 64% / 56% (Llama / Qwen). The reason is the prompt: the decision guide restates the policy’s covered and not-covered lists, so the judge has the rules even without retrieval (tested below). Without retrieval the citations are made up: both models still cited a clause in every case, almost always BPR-02, the example ID in the prompt; the check removes them and escalates the case. In the agent-driven design Llama searched in {ls} of cases and Qwen in {qs}, at {la_calls} LLM calls a case instead of 1.8; Gemini searched only when needed (3 of 10 probe cases) and matched the per-gap design on those 10 (9 right each). So we keep per-gap retrieval as the default: as accurate, one LLM call cheaper, and predictable; the tool stays as a fallback.
risk_invented: 0% in the agent’s final answers with all three tested models. Before the check Qwen cited a clause it was not shown (BPR-05) in 22% of judged cases; the check removed it and escalated them. Gemini’s baseline 0%
risk_model: Local 8B models: 52–54% and refund nearly everything; Gemini 90%. The app’s OpenAI fallback is untested, so its answers are marked as fallback
recommendation: Recommendation to Carousell (as in the video): ready for a staff-assist pilot with Gemini as the judge, not for automatic decisions, and not with a small local model. A pilot would measure average time to resolve a dispute, the share of decisions overturned on appeal, and the share of orders using ‘Buy’.
slides_eval_row: Data; 90% vs 88% (a tie on judgement) and the eligibility gain; the judge models (Gemini stays; local models refund almost everything)
rubric_intro: The decision guide restates the policy’s covered and not-covered lists, so the judge has the rules even without retrieval. A rubric-only guide (--guide rubric) keeps only our outcome rubric, so what is covered has to come from the retrieved clauses. Gemini was run on the first 25 test cases to save the free quota; they are all clear cases, so the borderline ones are not covered.
rubric_found: The local models cannot tell us: every 8B variant lands at 52–64% (a spread of 6 cases) and gets only 23–38% of seller wins right, whatever the prompt holds. For Gemini, retrieval can replace the restated policy (23 of 25 either way); without retrieval it declined two missing-accessory claims (G008, G043) that the policy covers, and it could cite nothing, so every case went to a person. So on this test set retrieval is not what makes the decisions accurate (Gemini mostly knows the rules). Its value is grounding every recommendation in a clause staff can check, putting coverage the model would miss in front of it, and letting a policy change be handled by re-indexing the text. A larger corpus would make retrieval matter more.
timeline_openai: Comparison kept to Gemini and the two local models; OpenAI only keeps the cloud app available
status_not_done: Not done yet: a person’s check of the citations and double-labelling some cases to measure agreement between labellers.
model_row_openai: Fallback only: the app uses it when a Gemini call fails. Unpaid key on OpenAI’s free usage tier (about 50 requests a day); not tested on our test set
